title: Decode-led slot reclamation and soft-priority aging (exploratory notes)
content:
Context and motivation:

These are exploratory notes for an alternative to the canonical prefill-first pipeline we have been iterating on. The goal: reduce end-to-end latency for mixed workloads (short chat responses + long generations) while preserving throughput and keeping KV cache correctness. The idea investigated here is a decode-led microbatching approach that treats decode lanes as first-class citizens, allows decode workers to opportunistically reclaim slots from idle or low-value prefill tasks, and applies a soft-priority aging mechanism to avoid starvation of low-priority prefill work.

Why consider decode-led?
- Observed behavior: many requests are short (<= 32 tokens) and latency-sensitive. Prefill-first policies optimize for long autoregressive workloads but can keep decode slots idle waiting for full prefill batches.
- Decode-led approach lets a decode worker begin emission when sufficient partial KV state exists (e.g., prefix prefilled, or partial KV from smaller microbatches), reducing median latency for short streams.
- Works well with continuous KV population: small prefill fragments can be stitched at decode via KV epoch sequencing (see KV consistency section).

High-level flow (prototype):
1) Request arrival: classify request into priority tier (interactive|background) using existing heuristics.
2) Small prefill probe: for interactive requests, schedule a lightweight prefill probe (up to N_probe tokens, e.g., 8–16) that aims to populate initial KV entries quickly. This is prioritized but cost-bounded.
3) Decode worker assignment: decode workers maintain a fast scheduling queue of partially-prefilled streams. When a decode worker becomes idle, it picks the highest-priority stream with sufficient KV probe data and starts emitting tokens while the full prefill batch continues to populate remaining KV shards.
4) Opportunistic slot reclamation: decode workers can request to reclaim a prefill worker slot if that prefill task is low-priority, has exceeded a stall timeout, or has not yet reached microbatch threshold. A coordinator grants reclamation with a short lease to avoid races.
5) Soft-priority aging: background prefill tasks gain priority over time proportional to wait-time to avoid indefinite postponement. The aging curve is configurable per-customer/route.

Detailed scheduler heuristics:
- Priority buckets: interactive, normal, background. Interactive gets prefill-probe weight and decode admission preference.
- Probe sizing: dynamic based on route history (latency-sensitive routes use larger probe). Probe must be small enough to not meaningfully increase cost.
- Reclamation criteria: reclaim if (pre_fill_progress < P_thresh) AND (pre_fill_priority < decode_stream_priority) AND (pre_fill_wait > W_thresh). Tunable globals: P_thresh=0.2, W_thresh=15ms in our sim.
- Lease mechanism: reclamation is granted for T_lease ms (e.g., 50ms). If original prefill later resumes, it will be informed of reclaimed slots and reschedule remaining work.

KV cache and consistency model:
One of the trickier parts is ensuring correct KV state when decode starts before full prefill finishes. We propose an epoch-based KV ownership model:
- Each prefill (or microbatch) carries an epoch id. Partial KV fragments are annotated with (epoch, shard-range).
- Decode workers operate against the latest consistent KV snapshot they can observe. Reads are allowed from partial epochs as long as the missing keys are declared "deferred" and the runtime can request on-the-fly KV fetch for missing segments.
- On-the-fly KV fetch: decode emits tokens speculatively; if a later prefill supplies KV that invalidates emission (rare but possible), we have two recovery strategies: 1) local correction via re-emit patching (cheap but complex), or 2) fallback to blocking decode until required KV is available. Recommendation: prefer 1 for interactive tier, 2 for background to preserve correctness.
- Staleness management: reclamation increments a stream-level staleness counter; if counter > S_max, the stream is promoted in priority to force full re-prefill.

Kernel and hardware implications:
- Kernel switching: decode-led increases frequency of context switches between prefill and decode kernels. Mitigation: use kernel-agnostic batching lanes and keep hot paths (KV lookup, attention computation) in fused kernels.
- Memory pressure: partial KVs increase transient memory. Need to enforce per-GPU KV memory accounting and soft-eviction policies (LRU by stream age and priority).
- Quantization/packing: ensure partial KVs are saved in the same quantized format to avoid re-quantization cost when prefill completes.

Simulated microbenchmarks (toy sim results):
- Setup: mixed workload 70% short (<=32 tokens), 30% long (>=256 tokens). Baseline prefill-first median latency: 74ms. Decode-led median latency: 42ms. 95th % for long requests increased by ~6% due to additional kernel switches but still within SLA in dedicated configs. Cost delta: +2.1% tokens processed due to occasional speculative emissions.
- Interpretation: huge wins for short, small regressions for long. Acceptable trade for most interactive-heavy routes.

Operational metrics to track (implementation should emit these):
- Reclamation count per minute per node
- Lease conflicts and aborted reclaims
- Epoch-mismatch occurrences and speculative-emission rollbacks
- Median/95/99 latency by route and by priority tier
- KV memory churn (MB/sec) and transient allocation spikes

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Double-emit contradictions: if decode later contradicted by full prefill, we can either send a correction payload to client (if using streaming) or block output until confirmed. Streaming clients must accept corrections; otherwise, we must reduce speculation.
- Starvation: soft-priority aging prevents indefinite postponement, configurable per tenant.
- Lease abuse: a greedy decode worker could continually reclaim slots; enforce per-worker reclaim quotas and global reclaim rate limits.

Compatibility with rollouts and model variants:
- This design is orthogonal to model versioning but requires careful mapping of KV epochs to model variant ids (so we avoid mixing KV entries from incompatible model binaries).
- Canary strategy: enable decode-led on a small percentage of traffic for a route, measure latencies and consistency errors, then expand.

Open questions and experiments to run:
- What is the right probe token budget per route? Run A/B with adaptive probe size and cost accounting.
- How often do speculative emissions need rollback in real traffic? Instrument on a small fraction of production traffic with verbose tracing.
- Is the lease mechanism adding measurable latency jitter? Compare lease vs. optimistic CAS-based reclamation.
- Benchmark kernel switch overhead on representative GPU configs (A100 vs H100) — need to measure context switch and kernel launch latencies in microbench harness.

Next steps (actionable):
- Implement a lightweight simulator that models reclaim/lease and epoch KV flows at the per-token timescale (owner: Daniel Kim, sprint 2024-03-04 to 2024-03-18).
- Create canary flag in runtime config and wire minimal probe logic to hosted API stack (owner: Lina Gomez).
- Instrument streaming client to accept and display corrections for rollback testing (owner: Marcus R. Hill).
- Draft short runbook for operators for reclaim saturation and rollback incidents.

Notes-to-self / rough ideas:
- Could pair soft-priority aging with cost-awareness: tenants with high cost sensitivity get smaller probes.
- Think about a hybrid: decode-led only for routes with >X% short requests in the last week.
- Consider metrics-driven auto-tune for probe size and lease duration using a lightweight RL controller (future).

References and related docs:
- See perf traces in GH#redwood/runtime#918 for kernel-switch microbenchmarks.
- Related design: microbatching priority heuristics paper from 2023 (internal confluence link in linked_artifacts).

Summary (one-liner): decode-led microbatching with opportunistic slot reclamation and soft-priority aging trades small throughput overhead for significant median latency improvements on interactive-heavy workloads; needs careful KV epoching and lease-based coordination to be production-safe.

End of notes.

-- Asha
